scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported record covers 1500 to 1530 and a broad polygon from eastern Ontario across much of southern Quebec. That polygon is not certified as the Algonquin homeland and should not be confused with the distribution of the entire Algonquian language family. No geometry was changed.

The narrative concerns Algonquin communities, with named examples from Kitigan Zibi and Pikwàkanagàn. It does not merge all Anishinaabe peoples or all Algonquian speakers. Local spellings are retained in source titles rather than normalized into a purported universal orthography.

The earliest dated institutional phase is the community-recorded 1603 encounter. This is not a founding date. The selected-year page must not fabricate a dated episode for the imported 1500 to 1530 interval from later community practices.

The 1850 and 1900 phase boundaries are approximate contextual divisions. The Kitigan Zibi page uses 1851 for formal reserve establishment, while Morrison describes the wider administrative process as 1851 to 1854. The card avoids collapsing that process into an unsupported single legal event.

Morrison’s 2005 historical report is explicitly a research draft. Its archaeological discussion is a synthesis referring to excavation literature, not a newly inspected excavation report. The card distinguishes documented materials and exchange from the interpretation of ethnic continuity. No exact modern ethnonym is assigned to every ancient find.

Morrison’s material-culture report was prepared for the Algonquin Nation Secretariat and interpreters at Fort Temiscamingue. The answered sections on housing, snowshoes and containers were read; later question lists are not treated as verified answers. No unsupported lifetime or performance figure for canoes is repeated.

The museum’s 2019 field account was read through its complete indexed text after the live page returned 403. Its named collection makers and direct workshop observations are distinguished from a full catalog or excavation record. The 1970s revival date is approximate and does not imply previous extinction of the craft.

Kitigan Zibi’s chiefs page contains a wrong 1910 starting date for the First World War and repeated paragraphs under different chiefs. Those passages are not used for wartime chronology or assigned uniquely to a chief. The Pakinawatik and Cayer accounts are attributed to the community history.

The school brochure identifies itself with the 1980 to 2010 anniversary, despite its 2021 upload path. Its opening date, historical partial immersion description and named 2009 art exhibition are read as dated evidence, not as current staffing or program promises.

Government population totals, reserve counts and current officeholders are omitted. No legal determination about pending land claims or modern territorial jurisdiction is made. Independent historical review, border assessment and depth certification remain pending.
